To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the optimum pilot spacing for PACE is determined by the sampling theorem and the pilot boost is given by a function of the pilot spacing, the channel bandwidth and the channel Doppler frequency.

the maximum capacity of pilot-aided MIMO-OFDMA is achieved with pilots spaced according to the Nyquist sampling rate and boosted in power, if the channel is perfectly known at the receiver and if the pilot symbols are used as training sequences for the estimation.

for pilot-aided MIMO-OFDMA with perfect interpolation, the optimal pilot spacing equals the sampling interval and the pilot gain equals the SNR, whereas for imperfect interpolation, pilot allocation can be determined by the particular estimator.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the capacity of pilot-aided MIMO-OFDMA systems, and the optimum pilot grid is derived for a variety of estimators.

the following aspects: (i) We present a general capacity framework for MIMO-OCFDM systems with pilot-aided estimation of time-variant frequency-selective fading channels, which is based on the concept of mutual information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pilot spacing is not critical, but the power allocation of the pilot symbols is of utmost importance for capacity.
the optimum pilot grid is a compromise between the pilot grid with minimum pilot overhead and the pilot grid with maximum equidistance.
the optimum pilot placement is achieved by a pilot spacing equal to the channel coherence interval and pilot boosting equal to the square-root of the number of subchannels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pilot-aided MIMO-OFDMA systems with perfect channel knowledge at the receiver and without channel knowledge at transmitter can be optimized in terms of pilot allocation.
for a given pilot grid and channel estimation method, the capacity of the system can be determined by the proposed analytical framework.
pilot allocation for PACE can be optimized in the same way as the allocation of subcarriers for OFDM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pilot overhead can be reduced significantly without sacrificing the capacity of MIMO-OCFDM.
the pilot allocation for PACE is not a one-shot problem, and that the optimal pilot allocation is dependent on the estimator and its parameters.
the pilot grid for PACE can be dimensioned in a data rate optimal fashion.
